holidays.name: National Beer Day
holidays.description: Raise a frosty mug to the end of a very dry era. This day celebrates beer in all its foamy forms, from crisp lagers to chocolatey stouts.
holidays.origin: It marks April 7, 1933. On that day the Cullen-Harrison Act took effect and made beer with low alcohol content legal again in the United States, near the end of Prohibition. The day was later popularized by beer fans, and it has become an annual toast.
holidays.funFact: Crowds reportedly gathered outside breweries at midnight in 1933, and trucks of beer were rushed to cities such as New York. Prohibition itself didn't fully end until December 1933.

holidays.name: No Housework Day
holidays.description: This is an official excuse to put down the mop, ignore the dishes, and let the dust bunnies live in peace for 24 hours. Today, doing nothing around the house counts as a valid way to celebrate.
holidays.origin: It's an unofficial observance, and its origin is unclear. It has long been a favorite among people who would rather relax than clean.
holidays.funFact: Whatever you skip today will still be waiting on April 8, so the dust bunnies are the only ones who truly come out ahead.

holidays.name: International Beaver Day
holidays.description: A day to honor nature's busiest engineer. Beavers build dams that create wetlands, help prevent floods, and provide habitat for countless other species.
holidays.origin: The day honors the birthday of Dorothy Richards, known as the Beaver Woman of Canada, who studied beavers for decades. It is observed by wildlife lovers and conservationists.
holidays.funFact: A beaver's orange teeth are colored by iron in the enamel, which makes them stronger, and they never stop growing.
